title: The Mind Like the Wind
word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
hook: Arjuna tells Krishna the mind can't be held. Krishna agrees, then tells him how
carry: evenness is yoga, and evenness is health
tomorrow: the roosters crow in Dvaraka. what does Krishna do first?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salt in the water: prakriti and vikriti describe a nature and a day, and tat tvam asi, you are that.

On the battlefield, in the sixth chapter of the Gita, Krishna has just described the yogi: still, the mind steady as a lamp in a place with no wind. And Arjuna, honest as ever, pushes back. Krishna, he says, this yoga of evenness you describe, I can't see it lasting. The mind is restless, stormy, strong and stubborn. Holding it seems as hard as holding the wind. It's one of the most human moments in the whole book. And Krishna doesn't tell him he's wrong.
screen: `A LAMP WHERE NO WIND BLOWS.` → `ARJUNA: THE MIND IS LIKE WIND.` → `KRISHNA DOESN'T ARGUE.`

segments.voice: No doubt, Krishna says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But it can be held, by practice, abhyasa, and by letting go, vairagya. Earlier in the same chapter he's said what that practice looks like day to day. Yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, or not at all; not for the one who sleeps too much, or stays awake too long. It's for the one who is moderate in food and rest, in work, in sleep and waking. Arjuna's word for it was samya, evenness. Earlier, the Gita says it in three words: samatvam yoga uchyate. Evenness is called yoga. Now set a line from the Ashtanga Hridaya beside it: illness is the doshas uneven; health is the doshas even. The same word, samya. Health isn't one dosha driven out. Vata, the moving one, still moves the breath; pitta still digests; kapha still holds you together. It's the three even with each other. And the restless mind Arjuna describes, blowing about like wind? Wind is just what vata means. The spiritual teaching and the medical one meet on the same wire: not the heroic extreme, but evenness, kept by small corrections, again and again. That's the Hindu answer to the all-nighter. The Gita doesn't praise the student who never sleeps; it says that path doesn't hold. Judging an imbalance in the body is a physician's work, and pain, fever or a worrying change goes to a doctor. What Krishna leaves you is the practice: catch the tilt, come back to the middle.
screen: `PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.` · `EVENNESS IS CALLED YOGA.` · `HEALTH: THE THREE DOSHAS EVEN.` · `CATCH THE TILT, COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and sway a little left, a little right, each sway smaller, until you settle near the center. Then let the mind rest on one thing. When it blows away like wind, bring it back, as the Gita says, again and again: that is abhyasa. If you pray, rest it on a name of God you love. If you don't, rest it on the breath.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing. Today, one word in two books: samya, evenness. In the Gita it is yoga; in the Ashtanga Hridaya, it is health.
Your line: evenness is yoga, and evenness is health. Catch the tilt, come back. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus who meditate often lean on Krishna's answer to Arjuna, practice and letting go, and on his call to moderation in food, sleep and waking; Ayurveda's classical definition of health as the doshas in balance uses the same word, samya, evenness. On this path it is used only for noticing, alongside medical care.

original.note: Sanskrit samya: evenness. Arjuna calls Krishna's teaching the yoga of evenness; the Ashtanga Hridaya calls the doshas in samya health.

trapdoor: what you thought: a holy life means extreme effort, little sleep, pushing past the body.
what it means: the Gita calls evenness yoga, and Ayurveda calls the doshas' evenness health. the extreme doesn't hold.

what a scholar hears: samatvam yoga uchyate (Gita 2.48), and rogas tu dosha-vaishamyam, dosha-samyam arogata, 'illness is the doshas uneven; health is the doshas even' (Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 1.20).
